note: The centurion's words are close in both: {mt 8:8 ἀλλὰ μόνον εἰπὲ λόγῳ καὶ ἰαθήσεται ὁ παῖς μου} (“only say the word and my servant will be healed”). But in Luke the centurion never meets Jesus; Jewish elders and then friends carry his messages. John has a similar long-distance healing of a {jn 4:46 βασιλικὸς} (“royal official”) whose **son** is ill, also at Capernaum. Matthew's *pais* can mean either “servant” or “boy”.

Only Luke tells this raising, and he models it on Elijah raising a widow's son (1 Kings 17). The last clause, {lk 7:15 ἔδωκεν αὐτὸν τῇ μητρὶ αὐτοῦ} (“he gave him to his mother”), is word for word the Septuagint of 1 Kings 17:23, and the crowd draws the conclusion: {lk 7:16 Προφήτης μέγας ἠγέρθη ἐν ἡμῖν} (“a great prophet has arisen among us”). Here, too, Luke's narrator first calls Jesus simply {lk 7:13 ὁ κύριος} (“the Lord”).

Two sharp exchanges shared nearly word for word, including {mt 8:20 ὁ δὲ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἔχει ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνῃ} (“the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head”) and the shocking {mt 8:22 ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς} (“let the dead bury their own dead”). Luke adds a third would-be follower who wants to say goodbye at home, echoing Elisha's call in 1 Kings 19, and a farming proverb: {lk 9:62 ἐπιβαλὼν τὴν χεῖρα ἐπ ἄροτρον} (“putting a hand to the plow”).

Compare the disciples' cry in each Gospel. In Mark it is a reproach: {mk 4:38 Διδάσκαλε οὐ μέλει σοι ὅτι ἀπολλύμεθα} (“Teacher, don't you **care** that we are perishing?”). Matthew turns it into a prayer: {mt 8:25 Κύριε σῶσον} (“**Lord**, save us”). Luke uses his own word, {lk 8:24 Ἐπιστάτα ἐπιστάτα} (“Master, Master”), a title found only in Luke in the New Testament. Mark's sleeping Jesus has a detail the others drop: he is on {mk 4:38 τὸ προσκεφάλαιον} (“the cushion”).

Mark's demon gives its name as {mk 5:9 Λεγιὼν} (*Legiōn*), a Latin loanword for a Roman army unit, and the swine number {mk 5:13 δισχίλιοι} (“about two thousand”). Matthew cuts Mark's twenty verses to seven, moves the scene to {mt 8:28 τῶν Γαδαρηνῶν} (“the Gadarenes”), and doubles the demoniac to {mt 8:28 δύο δαιμονιζόμενοι} (“two”). He doubles in the same way with blind men (9:27, 20:30). Manuscripts disagree over the place name in all three Gospels.

Mark places the bleeding woman **inside** the story of Jairus's daughter, a “sandwich” technique he uses often. Mark's father says {mk 5:23 Τὸ θυγάτριόν μου ἐσχάτως ἔχει} (“my little daughter is at the point of death”). In Matthew, who compresses the story, she has {mt 9:18 ἄρτι ἐτελεύτησεν} (“just died”). Mark keeps the Aramaic {mk 5:41 Ταλιθα κουμ}. Luke tones down Mark's jab that the woman {mk 5:26 ὑπὸ πολλῶν ἰατρῶν} (“under many doctors”) only got worse.

Found only in Matthew, this story closely resembles his later healing of two blind men at Jericho (20:29–34, Mark's Bartimaeus): two men, the same cry {mt 9:27 Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς υἱὲ Δαυίδ} (“have mercy on us, Son of David”), and a healing by touch. Many scholars see it as a doublet that Matthew placed here so that “the blind see” has already happened when Jesus answers John the Baptist in chapter 11.

Another short story found only in Matthew, and another apparent doublet: it reappears, expanded, at 12:22–24, where it launches the Beelzebul controversy. Here the crowd's verdict, {mt 9:33 Οὐδέποτε ἐφάνη οὕτως ἐν τῷ Ἰσραήλ} (“never has anything like this been seen in Israel”), closes Matthew's section of ten miracles (chapters 8–9) that follows the Sermon on the Mount: Jesus as Messiah in word, then in deed.

One of the densest clusters of minor agreements (52). Mark lets the missionaries take {mk 6:8 εἰ μὴ ῥάβδον μόνον} (“nothing **except a staff**”). Matthew and Luke **both** forbid even that: {mt 10:10 μηδὲ ῥάβδον} and {lk 9:3 μήτε ῥάβδον}. On the Two-Source view, a second, Q version of the mission overlapped Mark's. Only Matthew restricts the mission to Israel: {mt 10:6 πρὸς τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα οἴκου Ἰσραήλ} (“to the lost sheep of the house of Israel”).

Matthew builds his mission speech partly from material that Mark (and Luke) keep for the end-times discourse (Mark 13:9–13), moving warnings about councils, floggings and governors into the first mission. Only Matthew has the puzzling promise {mt 10:23 οὐ μὴ τελέσητε τὰς πόλεις τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου} (“you will not finish the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes”), long debated by interpreters.

Over half the words agree, but the arithmetic differs. In Matthew {mt 10:29 δύο στρουθία ἀσσαρίου} (“**two** sparrows for a penny”); in Luke {lk 12:6 πέντε στρουθία πωλοῦνται ἀσσαρίων δύο} (“**five** sparrows for two pennies”), which makes the fifth bird a free extra. Matthew's sparrow does not fall “apart from your Father”; Luke's is not “forgotten before God”. Luke alone addresses the disciples as {lk 12:4 τοῖς φίλοις μου} (“my friends”).

Matthew's image is military: {mt 10:34 οὐκ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰρήνην ἀλλὰ μάχαιραν} (“I came not to bring peace but a **sword**”). Luke's is the abstract {lk 12:51 διαμερισμόν} (“**division**”), and he prefaces it with a saying of his own: {lk 12:49 Πῦρ ἦλθον βαλεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν} (“I came to cast **fire** on the earth”). Both go on to describe a household split along generational lines, echoing Micah 7:6.

Luke's version is the harsher: anyone who does not {lk 14:26 μισεῖ τὸν πατέρα ἑαυτοῦ} (“**hate** his own father”) cannot be a disciple. Matthew softens it to a comparison: whoever {mt 10:37 ὁ φιλῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα ὑπὲρ ἐμὲ} (“loves father or mother **more than** me”). The Semitic idiom “love/hate” often means “prefer/put second”, so Matthew may be explaining rather than changing. Luke adds the parables of the tower-builder and the king going to war.

Matthew closes his mission speech with a chain of “receiving” sayings: {mt 10:40 Ὁ δεχόμενος ὑμᾶς ἐμὲ δέχεται} (“whoever receives you receives me”). Luke has a negative counterpart (“whoever rejects you rejects me”), and John has the same idea twice (13:20). The “cup of cold water” for {mt 10:42 ἕνα τῶν μικρῶν τούτων} (“one of these little ones”) is a saying Matthew takes from Mark 9:41.

John the Baptist, now in prison, asks {mt 11:3 Σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος} (“are you the one who is to come?”). Jesus answers with a list stitched from Isaiah 35 and 61. The list includes {mt 11:5 νεκροὶ ἐγείρονται} (“the dead are raised”), which is not in Isaiah, but a Dead Sea Scroll (4Q521) pairs raising the dead with good news for the poor in a list of the Messiah's works. Matthew and Luke agree in over 60% of their words here.

Long, close agreement (two-thirds of the words). Then a telling divergence: wisdom is vindicated {mt 11:19 ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων αὐτῆς} (“by her **deeds**”) in Matthew, but {lk 7:35 ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν τέκνων αὐτῆς} (“by all her **children**”) in Luke. Matthew's “deeds” loops back to “the deeds of the Christ” at 11:2. The obscure “violence” saying ({mt 11:12 βιάζεται}) appears in Luke in a completely different place (16:16).

Almost all of Luke's wording here is also in Matthew. The towns condemned include {mt 11:21 Χοραζίν} (Chorazin), which is never mentioned anywhere else in the Gospels, so no miracle performed there is recorded. A small window onto how much of Jesus' activity the Gospels do **not** narrate. The comparison with the pagan cities {mt 11:21 ἐν Τύρῳ καὶ Σιδῶνι} (“Tyre and Sidon”) is deliberately provocative.

Luke's version introduces the prayer with a uniquely emotional line: Jesus {lk 10:21 ἠγαλλιάσατο τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ} (“rejoiced in the Holy Spirit”). Then come 27 identical words in a row. The middle saying, {mt 11:27 οὐδεὶς ἐπιγινώσκει τὸν υἱὸν εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ} (“no one knows the Son except the Father”), sounds so much like John's Gospel that scholars call it the “Johannine thunderbolt”. Only Matthew adds {mt 11:28 Δεῦτε πρός με πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες} (“come to me, all who labor”).

Only Luke has this story of a woman who anoints Jesus' feet in a Pharisee's house. It resembles the anointing at Bethany that Mark, Matthew and John tell, which Luke omits. Its punchline is ambiguous: {lk 7:47 ἀφέωνται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι αὐτῆς αἱ πολλαί ὅτι ἠγάπησεν πολύ}, “her many sins are forgiven, **for** she loved much”. Is her love the cause of forgiveness or the evidence of it? The parable just before suggests the evidence. The text never names her.

Only Luke records that women traveled with Jesus and funded the mission: they {lk 8:3 διηκόνουν αὐτοῖς ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐταῖς} (“provided for them out of their own resources”). One is {lk 8:3 Ἰωάννα γυνὴ Χουζᾶ ἐπιτρόπου Ἡρῴδου} (“Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod's manager”), a link to the court of the ruler who killed John the Baptist. Joanna reappears at the empty tomb (24:10), named only by Luke.

Another dense cluster of minor agreements (52). Mark frames the dispute with Jesus' own family deciding {mk 3:21 ἐξέστη} (“he is out of his mind”), a line Matthew and Luke both omit. Both add a saying Mark lacks, in two versions: by {mt 12:28 πνεύματι θεοῦ} (“the **Spirit** of God”) or by {lk 11:20 δακτύλῳ θεοῦ} (“the **finger** of God”, echoing Exodus 8:19). Luke loves the Spirit, so most scholars think “finger” is the earlier wording.

One of the closest double-tradition passages: three-quarters of Matthew's words and almost all of Luke's are shared. The expelled spirit wanders {mt 12:43 δι ἀνύδρων τόπων} (“through waterless places”), the desert being a traditional home of demons, finds its old house swept and empty, and returns with seven others. Matthew applies it to {mt 12:45 τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ τῇ πονηρᾷ} (“this evil generation”).

A two-verse scene found only in Luke. A woman calls out a blessing on Jesus' mother: {lk 11:27 Μακαρία ἡ κοιλία ἡ βαστάσασά σε} (“blessed is the womb that carried you”). Jesus redirects it with {lk 11:28 Μενοῦν} (*menoun*), a particle that can mean “rather” or “yes, but even more”. Mary herself was earlier said to have heard God's word and kept it (1:38, 2:19), so the reply may include her rather than exclude her.

Matthew and Luke agree on most of the words, but they explain the “sign of Jonah” differently. In Matthew it is about **time in the grave**: {mt 12:40 τρεῖς ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς νύκτας} (“three days and three nights”). In Luke it is about **preaching**: Jonah was a sign {lk 11:30 τοῖς Νινευίταις} (“to the Ninevites”). Both end with {mt 12:41 πλεῖον Ἰωνᾶ ὧδε} (“something greater than Jonah is here”).

In Mark this scene closes a “sandwich” that opened with the family thinking Jesus mad (3:21). His family stand {mk 3:31 ἔξω} (“outside”), while the insiders are those who do {mk 3:35 τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ} (“the will of God”). Luke, who has just shown Mary as the model listener, drops the hostile framing and makes the saying a definition: {lk 8:21 οἱ τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ ἀκούοντες καὶ ποιοῦντες} (“those who hear the word of God and do it”).

Mark calls Herod Antipas {mk 6:14 ὁ βασιλεὺς Ἡρῴδης} (“**King** Herod”), but Rome never gave him that title. Matthew and Luke **both** correct it to {mt 14:1 ὁ τετραάρχης} (“the tetrarch”), the one minor agreement in this unit. Luke's Herod is puzzled rather than guilt-ridden ({lk 9:9 τίς δέ ἐστιν οὗτος}, “who is this?”) and “sought to see him”, a wish fulfilled only at the trial (23:8).

Mark tells this in vivid, novelistic detail, his longest story without Jesus in it. His Herod is torn: he {mk 6:20 ἡδέως αὐτοῦ ἤκουεν} (“listened to him gladly”). Matthew condenses it and makes Herod simply want John dead. Luke reports only the arrest (3:19–20) and skips the banquet entirely. The Jewish historian Josephus also records John's execution, but gives a political motive: Herod feared John's influence over the crowds.

The only miracle in all four Gospels. Mark's scene is painterly: the crowd sits {mk 6:39 συμπόσια συμπόσια} (“party by party”) on {mk 6:39 τῷ χλωρῷ χόρτῳ} (“the **green** grass”, springtime) in {mk 6:40 πρασιαὶ πρασιαὶ} (“bed by bed”, like a garden). John alone has the {jn 6:9 πέντε ἄρτους κριθίνους} (“five **barley** loaves”) and a boy, recalling Elisha's feeding in 2 Kings 4:42–44, and the crowd's attempt to {jn 6:15 ποιήσωσιν βασιλέα} (“make him king”).

Luke omits this story (it falls in his “great omission” of Mark 6:45–8:26). Mark's Jesus {mk 6:48 ἤθελεν παρελθεῖν αὐτούς} (“meant to **pass by** them”), language of God's self-revelation to Moses and Elijah. Mark ends with the disciples' {mk 6:52 ἡ καρδία πεπωρωμένη} (“hardened heart”). Matthew adds Peter walking on the water and ends with worship instead: {mt 14:33 Ἀληθῶς θεοῦ υἱὸς εἶ} (“truly you are the Son of God”). John's Jesus says {jn 6:20 Ἐγώ εἰμι} (“I am”).

A short Markan summary that Matthew copies closely. The sick beg to touch even {mt 14:36 τοῦ κρασπέδου τοῦ ἱματίου αὐτοῦ} (“the fringe of his cloak”). The *kraspedon* is likely the tassel that the Law commands Israelites to wear (Numbers 15:38–39), so Jesus is pictured as an observant Jew. The same word appears in the healing of the bleeding woman (Matthew 9:20, Luke 8:44).

Mark explains Jewish purity customs at length for readers who don't know them ({mk 7:3 οἱ γὰρ Φαρισαῖοι καὶ πάντες οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι}, “for the Pharisees and **all** the Jews…”), and translates {mk 7:11 Κορβᾶν}. Matthew, writing for Jewish Christians, drops the explanation. Mark's narrator draws a radical conclusion, {mk 7:19 καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα} (“declaring all foods clean”). Matthew omits it too, keeping the debate about hand-washing, not the food laws.

Mark calls her a Greek Syrophoenician; Matthew uses an archaic biblical label, {mt 15:22 γυνὴ Χαναναία} (“a **Canaanite** woman”), and adds {mt 15:24 Οὐκ ἀπεστάλην εἰ μὴ εἰς τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα οἴκου Ἰσραήλ} (“I was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel”). In both, Jesus' {mk 7:27 τοῖς κυναρίοις} (“little dogs”) is turned back on him: {mk 7:28 καὶ τὰ κυνάρια ὑποκάτω τῆς τραπέζης} (“even the dogs under the table…”). She is the one person in Mark who wins an argument with Jesus.

Mark's healing is physical and strange: fingers in the ears, spitting, touching the tongue, a sigh, and the Aramaic command {mk 7:34 Εφφαθα ὅ ἐστιν Διανοίχθητι} (“*Ephphatha*, that is, be opened”). Matthew and Luke both omit this story, and both also omit Mark's other healing with saliva (8:22–26). Matthew replaces it with a general summary of healings on a mountain. Perhaps they disliked techniques that looked like a folk healer's.

A second feeding, shared by Mark and Matthew only. The details differ: seven loaves, four thousand people, and {mk 8:8 ἑπτὰ σπυρίδας} (“seven **large baskets**”, *spyris*), against twelve *kophinoi* in the first feeding. Mark keeps the two basket words distinct when Jesus later quizzes the disciples (8:19–20). Many scholars think two versions of one event, but in Mark the doubling is meaningful, and the disciples still don't understand.

Mark's Jesus refuses outright: {mk 8:12 εἰ δοθήσεται τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ σημεῖον}, a Hebrew oath formula meaning “no sign **shall** be given”. Matthew adds an exception, {mt 16:4 εἰ μὴ τὸ σημεῖον Ἰωνᾶ} (“except the sign of Jonah”), repeating his own earlier saying (12:39). Luke's parallel is a different saying about reading the weather: {lk 12:56 τὸν δὲ καιρὸν τοῦτον πῶς οὐκ οἴδατε δοκιμάζειν} (“why can't you read **this** time?”).

Three Gospels, three interpretations of the “leaven”. Mark leaves it a riddle: {mk 8:15 τῆς ζύμης τῶν Φαρισαίων καὶ τῆς ζύμης Ἡρῴδου} (“the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod”). Matthew explains it as {mt 16:12 τῆς διδαχῆς τῶν Φαρισαίων καὶ Σαδδουκαίων} (“the **teaching** of Pharisees and Sadducees”). Luke says it is {lk 12:1 ὑπόκρισις} (“**hypocrisy**”). Mark's scene ends with an unanswered question to the uncomprehending disciples.

The only healing in the Gospels that takes two attempts. After the first touch the man says {mk 8:24 Βλέπω τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ὅτι ὡς δένδρα ὁρῶ περιπατοῦντας} (“I see people; they look like trees, walking”). Matthew and Luke both omit it. In Mark it is placed just after Jesus asks the disciples {mk 8:18 ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντες οὐ βλέπετε} (“having eyes, do you not see?”) and just before Peter half-sees who Jesus is: a parable in action.
